title: Generics
description: Write functions and types that work across many types while preserving full type information.

challenges.title: What do generics solve?
challenges.description:
What is the main advantage of `function identity<T>(v: T): T` over `function identity(v: any): any`?

  A)  It runs faster at runtime
  B)  The return type is known — TypeScript can check code that uses the result
  C)  It prevents the function from being called with wrong arguments
  D)  It removes the need for type annotations everywhere else
challenges.whyMatters: Generics are the key to writing reusable, type-safe utilities — without them, you either duplicate code or lose type information.
hints: Think about what TypeScript can tell you about the return value of each version

choices.label: A)  It runs faster at runtime
B)  The return type is known — TypeScript can check code that uses the result
C)  It prevents the function from being called with wrong arguments
D)  It removes the need for type annotations everywhere else

challenges.title: Identity and first element
challenges.description:
Write a generic function `identity<T>(value: T): T` that returns whatever it receives.

Then write `firstItem<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined` that returns the first element of an array.
challenges.whyMatters: Identity and first-element functions are the simplest generics — master the syntax here and every other generic will click faster.
hints: Declare a type parameter between the function name and the parameter list using angle brackets — both the parameter type and return type should reference that same type parameter
Array element type: T[] means an array of T, so the first element is type T

challenges.title: Generic wrapper interface
challenges.description:
Write a generic interface `Wrapper<T>` with a single field `value: T`.

Then write:
- `wrap<T>(value: T): Wrapper<T>` — wraps a value
- `unwrap<T>(wrapped: Wrapper<T>): T` — returns the inner value
challenges.whyMatters: The Wrapper pattern appears everywhere — Optional/Maybe types, Result<T, E> types, Promise internals. Learn the generic interface syntax here.
hints: wrap needs to return an object literal that satisfies Wrapper<T> — the interface tells you what field name to use
unwrap accesses a field on the wrapped object — same as reading any property from an interface

challenges.title: Generic constraints
challenges.description:
Write two constrained generic functions:

`getLength<T extends { length: number }>(value: T): number` — returns the length of anything with a length property.

`getLongest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T): T` — returns whichever of a or b is longer (return a if equal).
challenges.whyMatters: Constraints let you narrow what T can be — essential when your function needs specific properties from T without losing the generic type.
hints: The constraint is already written in the function signature — you just need to use the .length property in the body
getLongest compares two lengths and returns one of the inputs — a ternary expression fits well here

challenges.title: typeof and type predicates
challenges.description:
Write `typeOf<T>(value: T): string` that returns the JavaScript typeof string for any value.

Then write `isString(value: unknown): value is string` — a type predicate that narrows the type. Use `unknown` instead of a generic here — it accepts anything and is the correct type for narrowing.

Note: for null, typeof returns 'object' — that's correct JavaScript behaviour.
challenges.whyMatters: Type predicates are how generic code hands specific type knowledge back to the caller — TypeScript narrows the type in the if-branch automatically.
hints: typeOf just needs the built-in typeof operator — the same one you use in plain JavaScript
isString returns a boolean — but the return type annotation is a type predicate, check the concept card

challenges.title: Generic API response
challenges.description:
Write a generic interface `ApiResponse<T>` with:
- `data: T`
- `status: number`
- `error?: string`

Then write:
- `success<T>(data: T): ApiResponse<T>` — creates a 200 response
- `failure<T>(error: string): ApiResponse<T | null>` — creates a 500 response with null data
challenges.whyMatters: ApiResponse<T> is the single most common generic interface you'll write — every typed HTTP client wraps responses this way.
hints: Both functions return an object that satisfies ApiResponse — fill in the fields the interface requires
failure always has null data — look at the return type T | null to understand why that's valid

challenges.title: Multiple type parameters
challenges.description:
Write three functions with multiple type parameters:

`pair<A, B>(a: A, b: B): [A, B]` — creates a tuple from two values.

`swap<A, B>(pair: [A, B]): [B, A]` — returns a new tuple with the two elements swapped.

`mapFirst<A, B, C>(pair: [A, B], fn: (a: A) => C): [C, B]` — takes a tuple and a function. Calls the function with the first element, returns a new tuple with the result and the original second element unchanged.

Note: `fn: (a: A) => C` means fn is a function you receive as a parameter — call it with `fn(something)` to get a value back.
challenges.whyMatters: Multiple type parameters let you track multiple independent types through a transformation — tuples, Result<T, E>, and key-value pairs all need this.
hints: All three functions return a tuple — a fixed-length array literal like [x, y]
mapFirst receives a function fn — call it with the first element to transform it, keep the second as-is

challenges.title: keyof and indexed access
challenges.description:
Write two functions using `keyof`:

`getProperty<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]` — safely reads any property.

`pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(items: T[], key: K): T[K][]` — extracts a field from every object in an array.
challenges.whyMatters: `keyof` is how you write type-safe property accessors and data extraction utilities — the kind you'd find in lodash, data mappers, or ORM layers.
hints: getProperty: K is constrained to be a valid key of T, so obj[key] is type-safe — just return it
pluck is getProperty applied to every item in an array — use .map()

challenges.title: Bring it together
challenges.description:
Write a generic `Repository<T extends { id: string }>` interface with:
- `findById(id: string): T | undefined`
- `findAll(): T[]`
- `save(item: T): void`
- `delete(id: string): boolean`

Then write `createRepository<T extends { id: string }>(): Repository<T>` that stores items in memory using a Map.
challenges.whyMatters: Generic repositories are one of the most common patterns in typed backends — you define the shape once and get a type-safe store for any entity.
hints: Declare a Map<string, T> inside createRepository — it's the private store all four methods share via closure
Each method maps directly to one Map operation — check the concept card for the Map API
